subject: Mathematics
title: Terminating and Recurring Decimals
summary: 1/4 = 0.25 stops, but 1/3 = 0.333… never does. The remainders of long division decide: a remainder of 0 stops it, a returning remainder makes it repeat.
keyPoints: Remainders are always **less than the divisor**, so if 0 never comes, one must come back → the digits **repeat**.
In lowest form, a denominator with **only 2s and 5s** terminates; any other prime factor repeats.
Rational ⇔ terminating or recurring; neither ⇒ irrational.

blocks.p: At every step of long division a remainder is left. If it becomes **0**, the division stops. Dividing by q, the remainder can only be 0 to q − 1, so if 0 never comes, some remainder **must come back**, and from then on the digits repeat.

blocks.alt: Long division of 1 by 7 with the remainders listed
blocks.caption: The remainder 3 returns at step 7.

blocks.alt: A wheel of remainders 0 to 6 with the loop 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1
blocks.caption: Only 7 possible remainders: a loop is unavoidable.

blocks.formula: p/q in lowest form terminates ⇔ q = 2ᵐ × 5ⁿ

quiz.q: Which fraction has a non-terminating recurring expansion?
Why must the decimal of 1/7 repeat?
options: Remainders can only be 0–6 and 0 never comes, so one returns
quiz.explain: With finitely many possible remainders and no 0, a remainder must recur.
It neither terminates nor repeats, so it is irrational.

simulation.reason: Dividing any p/q and watching the remainders land on a wheel shows why some decimals stop and others must repeat; students can test their own fractions, which a fixed video cannot offer.
simulation.objective: Divide any fraction and see whether its decimal terminates or repeats, and why.
instructions: Set p and q with the + and − buttons, or pick an example.
Press Divide and follow the long division step by step.
Watch the remainders light up on the wheel.
See whether the remainder reaches 0 (terminates) or comes back (repeats).
